lesson.title: Meiosis II: Splitting the Sister Chromatids
lesson.summary: Meiosis II divides the two haploid cells from meiosis I once more, separating sister chromatids using essentially the same mechanics as mitosis to yield four haploid cells in total.
lesson.body:
Meiosis II picks up where meiosis I left off, with two haploid cells, each carrying one chromosome from every original homologous pair, but each of those chromosomes still doubled into two sister chromatids. No DNA replication happens between the two divisions, meiosis II simply finishes the job of separating what meiosis I left joined.

The phases of meiosis II, prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II, and telophase II, follow a pattern that should look familiar, because mechanically they are essentially a standard mitotic division happening inside a haploid cell. At metaphase II, chromosomes line up individually along the metaphase plate rather than as paired tetrads, since each cell already contains only one member of each homologous pair. At anaphase II, the sister chromatids of each chromosome finally separate, pulled to opposite poles exactly as they would be in mitotic anaphase, and each is now considered its own full chromosome.

Telophase II and cytokinesis complete the process: nuclear envelopes reform around each set of separated chromosomes, and the cytoplasm divides. Because meiosis I already produced two cells and each of those now divides once more in meiosis II, the overall result of meiosis is four haploid cells from a single starting diploid cell, and thanks to crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis I, no two of the four are genetically identical.

The outcome looks different depending on which sex is producing the gametes, at least in humans and many other animals. In sperm production, cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm evenly at both meiotic divisions, so all four haploid products typically develop into functional sperm cells. In egg production, cytokinesis is dramatically unequal at both divisions: most of the cytoplasm, and the nutrients and organelles it contains, is retained by just one of the two cells produced at each step, while the other becomes a small, non-functional cell called a polar body that eventually degenerates. The result is that one diploid cell going through meiosis typically yields only a single functional egg, but that egg is well stocked with the cytoplasmic resources a future embryo will need.
